title: This Fishing Game Was Made with AI? — Six AI-Assisted Games

scenes.title: Start with the games
lines: Hello, this is Yamyam Coding. Fishing, futuristic racing, and predicting a god's next attack: how much did AI contribute to making these games?

We'll look at six games, their creator-reported development milestones, where they run, and the engines behind them. Along the way, we'll briefly introduce the AI tools and the jobs they handled. We'll distinguish quick initial versions from games refined over several weeks.
Let's begin on this little island, where you can see beneath the water.

scenes.title: I Just Wanted to Fish
lines: I Just Wanted to Fish lets you explore an island and fish. A character casts from the beach, with fish and coral visible in the shallow water. Small crabs also wander along the shore.

It is a PC game preparing for a Steam release, built in Unity 6. A game engine brings together functions such as controls, collisions and rendering. This project uses Unity's High Definition Render Pipeline, or HDRP, for high-fidelity rendering.
The creator reported almost three weeks of work. That describes progress at the time of the post, not a completed commercial release.

Let's briefly introduce the AI used here. Claude Opus 5.5 is an AI model from Anthropic. It can interpret requests and code, then write or revise code. This creator also used it to implement desired objects and movement.

Claude Code is the development tool, rather than the model name. It can read and edit project files, run commands and carry out development tasks. Opus interprets requests and produces code; Claude Code puts the model to work in a development environment.

MCP is a standard for connecting external tools. Blender MCP and Unity MCP connected AI-assisted tasks to those applications. Blender makes 3D models and animation; Unity assembles them into an interactive game.

Back on the beach, creating the character and crab, adding motion and arranging them among water and terrain all contribute to one scene. The creator designed the layout, supplied reference drawings and repeatedly revised the results.
The Steam disclosure also says no AI is used while playing. Using AI during development is different from having AI generate responses throughout gameplay.
While this is a Unity-based PC game, our next example is a small world you can enter through a browser.

scenes.title: Emberfall — Luminati
lines: This is Emberfall — Luminati. Its characters resemble pixel art, while houses and paths occupy a space you can view from different camera angles. It feels like a miniature village.

The game player and level editor are published at separate addresses. The player runs in a browser without a separate installation, where we verified character movement and camera rotation. The level editor provides terrain-height, object and lighting controls. Both links will be labeled separately in the description.

The editor identifies itself as Luminati and names Three.js as its foundation. Three.js is a graphics library: reusable functions for drawing 3D scenes in a browser. Game rules and editing functions are built on top to make this village editable and interactive.
The exact AI model version and total development time could not be confirmed from a creator primary source. We'll separate the visible technical foundation from the unverified development history.
So far, we've looked at a small world's appearance and space. The next fishing game shows an ongoing effort to fill a world with story and systems.

scenes.title: Nightshoal
lines: Nightshoal also features fishing and exploration, but has a different atmosphere. Waterways wind between cliffs and forests as a boat passes through. Its creator continues adding quests, story, fishing and inventory systems.

This work-in-progress game is downloaded and run on a Windows PC. The public build is described as a pre-demo, and the engine is Godot. The 3D space and game behavior are assembled in a Godot project.
The public development update marks week eleven. The creator named Claude Opus 5.5 for recent work, with Codex Astra used earlier.

Codex is OpenAI's coding agent. An agent is a tool that can carry out linked tasks, such as editing files and checking the results. In the creator's account, Codex is the development tool and Astra names the AI model used.

Code-focused AI wasn't the only tool filling this world. The creator used Tripo AI for complex 3D models. Tripo generates models from text or images. Placement, scale and behavior still need to be integrated into the game.

The creator also used OpenAI's image-generation API. An API lets software request a generation service. This service creates or edits images from prompts or reference images; the exact image model used for this game was not disclosed.

What about sound? ElevenLabs' sound-effects generation creates requested sounds from written descriptions. The creator used Stable Audio for music, describing its desired mood and style. Effects tied to individual actions and music carrying a scene serve different jobs.

These models, images and sounds must work together in one game. Blender MCP was also used for simpler models, and the creator describes ongoing revisions to the map and features. Someone still decides what to build, checks the results and fixes mismatches.
Here, several tools helped fill a world. In the next game, we'll see what happens when movement and immediate visual feedback become the focus.

scenes.title: VECTOR: Anti-Gravity Racing
lines: In VECTOR: Anti-Gravity Racing, floating craft replace wheels. You navigate corners, cross boost sections and race other craft.
This is another browser game played on a web page. It uses the same Three.js graphics library we saw earlier, this time for high-speed racing rather than a miniature village.

Rendering uses WebGPU, an interface that lets a browser access graphics-processing hardware. The creator also describes a WebGL 2 fallback where WebGPU is unavailable. These are graphics interfaces, rather than AI models or game engine names.

The creator describes coding through AI conversation and asking AI to use Blender for models. The exact development duration and AI model version remain unconfirmed, so we cannot attribute the result to one specific model.
Just as interesting as high speed is its opposite: a game that pauses time and asks you to think through each move.

scenes.title: AUGURY: Duel of the Gods
lines: AUGURY features dueling gods, but it isn't about rapidly pressing buttons. Time pauses while you choose a move. A green silhouette previews your destination, and committing advances the outcome. Predicting the opponent's choice is central.

It runs directly on an itch.io web page and is built with Phaser and TypeScript. Phaser is a 2D game framework with functions such as rendering and input. TypeScript is the programming language used to express game rules.

DreamLayer appears in the character and prop workflow. It is a creative AI agent that selects an image model and carries out a requested image task. It can also use a reference character to help produce further images of that character.

The development report also names an image-generation tool as ImageGen. The record shows image generation and editing, but that label alone does not identify an exact model. These image tools should be distinguished from the game framework.

Returning to character movement, generating a picture and making it work in a game are separate tasks. The creator removed backgrounds, prepared sizes and colors, and adjusted body and prop layering and movement, using Python helpers and custom editing tools.
The total development duration could not be established from public records. What the report does show is the work of turning generated artwork into readable choices and combat.
That need for refinement is worth remembering when we look at the next short development milestone.

scenes.title: Rally Road Rash
lines: Rally Road Rash features dirt-track collisions, jumps and rockets. Its creator reported making an initial version in about three days.

It is a browser game published on Sandscape. Sandscape is a creation platform for requesting games in text, refining them visually or through code, and sharing them. The underlying engine for this game could not be confirmed from public material.

The creator used Opus 5.5 for vehicles and physics, and a model they called Astra 6 for visual refinement. GPT-6 Astra is an OpenAI model used for coding and complex problem-solving. The interesting point here is how the creator divided the work between models.

Another tool contributed vehicle geometry. Meshy generates 3D models from text or images. The creator reports using it for major vehicles and props, alongside simpler background objects created through code.
Those models still need collision and motion behavior. A vehicle jumping and landing combines its visible shape with game physics. Generating a model does not automatically finish its handling.

The creator also named ElevenLabs for music. Separately from the sound-effects feature discussed earlier, the company offers music generation guided by descriptions of mood or genre. The specific music model version used here was not disclosed.

The creator edited levels personally and reported twenty-five years of experience. Motorcycle physics were still being refined. Three days describes that initial version; it doesn't guarantee anyone could achieve the same result in the same time.
Placed side by side, the six games reveal a change more clearly than their development-time numbers alone.

scenes.title: How far have things come?
lines: Some games use engines such as Unity and Godot, while others run in browsers using Three.js or Phaser. The foundation that runs a game and the AI that helped make it have different roles.
AI contributions extend beyond code to 3D models, images, animation work, effects and music. Alongside the model name, it helps to ask what was generated and what people selected and revised.
This report is based on public material checked on October 18, 2026. Links to all six games and their development records will be in the description. Which one would you like to try?
